first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, so I read it properly. The opening is calm and grown-up, no silly slang, and I liked that they say where their information comes from. When it promised to cover 'the travel advice and legal steps the listicles skip' I knew I would read to the end, because that's the part I actually worry about.

journey.quote: we have been plain about which details come from UNESCO, the Smithsonian or parish sources and which are simply often told.
journey.reaction: Good. I'd rather be told 'we're not sure' than be sold a fairy tale. That's a firm I could take seriously.

journey.quote: treat what follows as a map to talk through with your parents and grandparents, not a rulebook.
journey.reaction: Nice to be included rather than talked around. It also gives me something to discuss with my daughter over dinner.

journey.quote: It asks couples to make contact at least eight months ahead and to confirm the priest and church before booking anything else.
journey.reaction: That's exactly the kind of practical warning I want. I'll make sure we don't put down a venue deposit before the church is confirmed.

journey.section: Lavash, honey and the broken plate at the door
journey.quote: decide in advance where the "door" will be (a villa entrance, a ballroom foyer) and who will stand in the mother-in-law's place if she cannot travel.
journey.reaction: Sensible, and it shows they've thought about older family not being able to fly. But that's where it stops. Nothing about how the grandparents would actually cope with the trip itself.

journey.quote: Australia has no embassy or consulate in Armenia, and consular help comes from the Australian Embassy in Moscow.
journey.reaction: Well, that worries me. If my mother falls ill over there, who do I ring? Moscow? I'm glad they told me straight, but the article doesn't say what Wedded Wonderland would do about it.

journey.quote: male dual nationals aged 18 to 28 may be liable for military service. Raise this with any dual-national groom or relative at the first planning conversation, not at the airport.
journey.reaction: I would never have thought of that. This alone is worth forwarding to my husband. It tells me the people writing this know the real risks.

journey.section: Civil registration and the church wedding
journey.quote: We could not read an official Armenian source on this. Check with Armenia's civil registry and the Armenian embassy, including any fees, before you set a date.
journey.reaction: Honest, which I respect, but it leaves me with homework and no answer. I'd want to know whether someone would help us find out, and in what language the paperwork would be.

journey.section: Documents, translation and recognition at home
journey.quote: Ask the same registry and embassy about translation of your documents into Armenian, and about how your marriage will be recognised once you are home.
journey.reaction: Contracts and documents in another language are one of my big worries, so I'm glad it's raised. Again though, it's left to us.

journey.quote: You will have a single point of contact, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins; the legal and church paperwork stays with you, the registry and your priest.
journey.reaction: This is the sentence that matters most to me. One person, fee in writing, and they're honest about what they won't do. I'd still want to know who that person is and whether I can speak to them on the phone.

unanswered_questions: Who do we ring if something goes wrong on the day in Armenia, given consular help is in Moscow? Does the Wedded Advisor have someone on the ground?
Are deposits paid to suppliers in Armenia protected, and in what currency are quotes and contracts?
Will contracts with Armenian venues or suppliers be in English?
Can elderly guests with limited mobility manage the churches and venues around Yerevan? Is any help with transfers or accessible transport available?
Is travel insurance something the Wedded Advisor helps us sort out, or is that entirely on us?
Can I speak to the Wedded Advisor by phone before anything is booked, and will they have a name?
would_share_with: My husband, with the Smartraveller and dual-national paragraphs highlighted
My daughter, to talk about which customs we keep
My sister, who is helping with the grandparents' travel

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like one person to coordinate the venue, travel and suppliers around those answers, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: The 'fee agreed in writing' line pulls me in. I'd click if I knew it led to a phone call with a named person rather than a form that disappears into a sales funnel. I won't book anything without talking to someone first.

top_3_changes: Next to the Moscow consular line, add a sentence on what support the couple and their guests have on the ground if something goes wrong, so a parent knows who to ring.
Add one or two practical lines on elderly or less mobile guests travelling to Armenia: transfers, getting into old churches, travel insurance.
Near the CTA, say plainly that the first step is a conversation (ideally a phone call) with a real person, and mention how deposits and supplier contracts are handled.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent, practical, safety and money focused)
No invented brand facts; anything the page does not say is listed in unanswered_questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments treated as invisible
No invented problems; deferred business details and absence of prices not raised as must-fix

open_questions.question: Margaret's main gaps (who to ring in an emergency, deposit protection, elderly guest access) depend on business details that are deferred. Treat as nice-to-have unless the brand facts become available.

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is considering a wedding with Armenian customs, possibly in Armenia, which is why she sent the link.
Absence of prices is the house standard and is not counted against the article.
